vr-portfolio-1-demo-1-q05.backText:
Short quiz answer

A normal map perturbs the lighting normal to create the appearance of surface detail without changing geometry. Our corrugation normal map changes highlights; the emission map makes selected strips appear bright.

How our project does it

It changes the normal used in lighting, not the silhouette or geometry. RGB stores tangent-space directions and is interpreted as linear data. The corrugation texture changes visible highlights. An emission map marks a strip as bright; it does not illuminate surrounding geometry in this renderer.

Understand the idea

  • A normal is a direction perpendicular to a surface. Lighting uses it to decide how the surface faces the light.
  • Tangent-space normal-map RGB encodes direction relative to the textured surface. It is linear vector data, not colour that should receive an sRGB colour conversion.
  • The cabin can look ridged while keeping the same silhouette and triangle count. Emission does not cast light onto nearby surfaces in this renderer; the point/spot lights do that.

vr-portfolio-1-demo-1-q04.backText:
Short quiz answer

The custom cabin’s four wall quads each occupy one-quarter of the texture’s U range, with V running bottom-to-top. Separate wall vertices allow independent UVs and face normals.

How our project does it

cabin.js authors four tapered wall quads. Each wall's four UV corners occupy a quarter of the texture's U axis, with V from bottom to top. Adjacent geometric walls have separate vertices so they can have separate normal/UV values. Each quad is two indexed triangles. Floor/roof are separate meshes.

Understand the idea

  • UV coordinates are 2D addresses on a texture. U is horizontal and V is vertical; a 3D wall’s vertices tell the renderer which pixels to stretch across it.
  • Wall 0 uses U=0–0.25, wall 1 uses 0.25–0.5, wall 2 uses 0.5–0.75 and wall 3 uses 0.75–1. Each wall consists of two triangles.
  • Duplicating corner vertices across wall boundaries permits a UV seam and a different surface normal for each flat wall. The floor and roof are separate meshes.

vr-portfolio-1-demo-2-q02.backText:
Short quiz answer

FeedTrajectory predicts with the same forces and timestep as live play, then searches for an initial upward velocity that lands on the player’s half. That fixes short feeds without steering the ball or disabling the net.

How our project does it

The speed preset sets forward velocity. FeedTrajectory predicts the first table-height crossing using the same forces and timestep as play. If it lands too short, increase initial upward velocity; if too far, decrease it. Sixteen binary-search steps aim for z=0.85 on the player's half, and the result is cached per preset. Tests cover all 24 speed/spin/wind combinations against actual table/net colliders. No forces or net collision are disabled, and there is no steering after launch. A weak, low player return can still hit the net normally.

Understand the idea

  • The speed button controls the forward component, not the total 3D speed. A separate upward component determines airtime and the arc.
  • Sixteen binary-search iterations repeatedly halve the upward-velocity interval, aiming for the first table-height crossing at z=0.85 m.
  • Results are cached per preset, so the prediction is not repeated every frame. All 24 tested speed/spin/wind presets cleared the actual net collider; low player returns can still hit it.

vr-portfolio-1-demo-2-q05.backText:
Short quiz answer

Drag opposes air-relative velocity and grows with speed squared. Magnus lift acts perpendicular to spin and air-relative travel, so reversing spin changes the lift direction; our lift coefficient is deliberately bounded.

How our project does it

Drag opposes the ball's velocity relative to wind and scales with its speed squared, frontal area, density and Cd. Magnus lift points along ω×v and depends on spin ratio. Here the lift coefficient is capped at 0.6, a stated approximation. Positive/negative spin reverses lift direction. Real ball aerodynamics can be more complicated than this model.

Understand the idea

  • Air-relative velocity is ball velocity − wind velocity. Still air and a crosswind therefore produce different forces even if the ball’s world velocity initially matches.
  • Drag follows ½ρCdA|v|v with the opposite sign, divided by mass to get acceleration. Here ρ is air density, Cd is drag coefficient, and A=πr² is frontal area.
  • Magnus direction follows ω×v, a cross product. Our coefficient is min(0.6, 0.6r|ω|/|v|). This is an approximate bounded model, not a complete aerodynamic fit.

vr-portfolio-1-demo-2-q06.backText:
Short quiz answer

Tracked pose differences give paddle linear and angular velocity. Contact uses ball velocity relative to the moving paddle, including the rotational contribution ω×offset, so faster and differently directed swings change the return.

How our project does it

TrackedPose.Update calculates (current position − previous position)/deltaTime and angular change/deltaTime. The paddle is kinematic. Its contact-point velocity adds angular velocity cross the offset from controller to contact. The impulse is computed using ball velocity relative to that moving surface. Swing direction and racket orientation change the outgoing direction.

Understand the idea

  • Linear velocity is change in position ÷ elapsed time. Angular velocity describes how fast and around which axis the controller rotates.
  • A point at the paddle face can move faster than the controller origin because it is offset from the hand: contact velocity = hand velocity + ω×offset.
  • The paddle is kinematic: tracking dictates its pose, rather than simulated forces moving it. Surface-relative velocity, face orientation and contact friction determine the outgoing ball.

vr-portfolio-1-demo-2-q09.backText:
Short quiz answer

We check swept paths rather than only final overlaps: a sphere cast for world surfaces and a relative moving-paddle sweep for the racket. Four substeps also resolve the paddle’s changing orientation.

How our project does it

The ball moves as an explicitly simulated state. A sphere cast examines the complete old→new segment against world colliders. A relative sweep examines ball/paddle poses against the moving elliptical face; four substeps account for its changing orientation. Endpoint-only overlap would miss a ball that crosses a thin surface in one step. The kinematic Rigidbody's flag is not the entire contact method.

Understand the idea

  • Tunneling occurs when a fast ball is before a thin surface at one sample and beyond it at the next, with neither endpoint overlapping.
  • A sphere cast follows a sphere along the whole old→new segment. The custom paddle sweep considers relative ball/paddle motion and the racket’s elliptical face.
  • This is custom continuous detection. We do not claim the solution is simply a Rigidbody CCD checkbox, and smaller timesteps alone are not the whole method.

vr-portfolio-1-demo-4-q06.backText:
Short quiz answer

The original reference-space reset did not cancel yaw and could change height. The fix computes a yaw correction from the current world-facing direction and rotates the rig around the head, preserving position, height and hunt progress.

How our project does it

Requesting another local-floor reference space did not cancel the artificial turn; the student observed a small height change instead of a heading reset. The corrected action reads the current world forward vector and adds yaw atan2(forward.x, −forward.z) to face world −Z. It rotates around the head, compensating rig X/Z with the head's before/after position so a real tracking offset does not orbit into another location. It does not change Y, recalibrate height, replace the tracking reference space or reset the hunt. Height calibration is a separate button. Test it at the start with three right snap turns: the A RECEIVING ← → B TOOLS sign should return in front, with eye height unchanged.

Understand the idea

  • Starting-aisle forward is world −Z. Compute the correction using atan2(forward.x, −forward.z).
  • Record world head position before/after the rotation, then compensate the rig’s X/Z translation so an existing room-scale offset does not orbit.
  • This is heading reset, not replacing the tracking reference space, changing Y, recalibrating height or restarting the hunt.
  • At the starting location, the A RECEIVING ← → B TOOLS sign should return ahead after turning and resetting. That is a behavioral check, not proof of every device condition.
